newsitem.title: USA: Unfair tax laws hurt working wives.
newsitem.headline: Unfair tax laws hurt working wives.

text.p: The newest champion of working women could just be a male professor from southern California who says that tax laws adopted years ago "consciously penalise married working women" and it's time they were scrapped.

"The tax system was set up in the 1930s and 1940s with a traditional family in mind -- man as earner, woman as stay-at- home wife," said Edward McCaffery, a University of Southern California law professor and an authority on taxation.
That bias was kept in place even though the majority of women have since entered the work force, he said. There is a need for a new tax structure, one that he said incorporates "gender justice."

In his fascinating new book, "Taxing Women" (University of Chicago Press), McCaffery finds that many married women actually lose money by working because there is a tax bias in favour of single-earner families.

He says that the financial impact on working women, including a combination of taxes, Social Security and child expenses, are acting to push women out of the workforce, and in some cases, out of their marriages.

McCaffery analysed the tax rates for individuals and married people and found that when working couples file their returns jointly, current tax laws "make very literal the 'marginalization' of women."

He writes, "By adding together husband and wife, tax laws encourage families to look at the impact of the wife's earnings on both the family's bottom line and its general happiness. The wife's employment outside the home becomes marginal or discretionary..."

According to IRS data, McCaffery said, more than 97 percent of married couples continue to file jointly, with the lesser of the two wage earners, most often the woman, paying an inordinate percentage of income tax.

Comparing a married woman's salary of $30,000 to a single woman's salary of $30,000, under current tax rules McCaffery found that the married woman paid about $6,000 more in taxes. This is because her $30,000 income was added to her husband's (for example) $60,000 salary, putting the second salary into a much higher tax bracket than that of the single woman.
Under current rules, a married woman filing separately from her husband may not do much better than if had she filed jointly, McCaffery said.
The bias against two-earner families hits different income levels in different ways. The lower the joint income, the harder the hit against familes in general, he said from his office in Los Angeles.
However, for upper-income families, he said, the tax bias encourages married women to stay at home.

The wife of a well-paid executive can face an income tax rate of 30 percent, a Social Security tax of 8 percent, and state and local taxes of 10 percent. From what's left over must come payments for child care, often making the net earnings not worth the effort.
While taxes are a major part of the problem, a reworking of tax rules can be part of the solution, he said.
Prior to 1948, men and women filed separate returns and, McCaffery urged, "we should go back to individual filings so that the wife is entitled to her own zero bracket."
"The more the husband earns now, the more we tax the wife," he added. "That's kind of perverse." Most developed countries, he noted, have abolished joint tax filing.
The author recommends lowering tax rates across the board, with the biggest reductions for married women.

"This country could be richer, could be bigger, the pie would grow and would expand if we made it a little easier for women to work, if we made it a little easier to get child care, and if we lowered those high tax rates facing wives," the University of Southern California law professor asserted.
"It is unconscionable to leave this system in place, simply because it is now the status quo," McCaffery concluded.
(EDITORS: Sherwood Ross is a freelance writer who covers workplace issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Ross.)
